proposals.hypothesis: LiBr is a wide-gap (about 6 eV), electronically insulating Li-ion conductor. Its Br- anion is a softer, more reducible halide than O2- or F-, so it may form a more benign interphase with Li6PS5Cl than the P-O/S exchange seen for Li3PO4 or the F-driven reactions seen for LiF. Its halide framework also resembles the electrolyte's own halide chemistry, so the contact penalty should be lower than the oxide and fluoride cases. The main risk is Br- oxidation at 4.0 V against LiCoO2.
proposals.motivation: LiF gave the lowest penalty so far (0.189, bin 9). Li3PO4 (0.337) and Li2MgCl4 (0.310) were both worse, and both reacted with the sulfide electrolyte. A different halide anion may reduce the sulfide-contact penalty further.

proposals.hypothesis: Li8ZrO6 is a very Li-rich zirconate built on fully oxidized Zr4+, which is hard to reduce by the sulfide electrolyte. Its high Li2O content should lower the driving force for P-S/Cl exchange, which was the main failure mode for the phosphate, fluoride, chloride and bromide coatings. It is a wide-gap insulator and should be oxidatively stable against LiCoO2 at 4.0 V. The oxide family is partly explored, but this Zr-based, highly lithiated framework is chemically distinct from the Al/Si, B and P oxides tried so far.
proposals.motivation: LiAlSiO4 gave the lowest penalty so far (0.189, bin 9), but every tested coating still failed through sulfide-contact reactions. Li3BO3 gave the lowest contact penalty so far, so a related Li-rich borate with a more electropositive, reduction-resistant cation may lower the sulfide-contact driving force further. It should be a wide-gap insulator and oxidatively stable against LiCoO2 at 4.0 V.
